text:
Philip Rubin earned his BA in psychology and linguistics from Brandeis University in 1971, followed by a PhD in experimental psychology from the University of Connecticut in 1975 under Michael Turvey. His research integrates computational, engineering, linguistic, physiological, and psychological approaches to study embodied cognition, particularly focusing on the biological foundations of speech and language.
Rubin is well known for his pioneering work in speech technology, including foundational issues in speech production and perception. Key contributions include designing the Haskins articulatory synthesis program (ASY) and the Haskins sinewave synthesis program (SWS). He developed concepts for describing and controlling articulatory events, now known as speech gestures, and created the configurable articulatory synthesizer (CASY). Furthermore, he has made significant theoretical contributions, developing a dynamical systems/action theory perspective on speech that emphasizes the spatiotemporal coordination of global aspects of the system. He has also been involved in science administration, policy, and advocacy roles, including leadership positions at the National Science Foundation and the Office of Science and Technology Policy in the Executive Office of the President of the United States.
